passages.source_text: πλὴν ἵνα οὕτως ταῦτα γένηται, ἐπενόησα ὄνειρον πλάσασθαι ὡς δὴ τινὸς νύκτωρ ἐπιστάντος μοι καὶ εἰρηκότος Γύναι, ἐξαυτῆς ἅμα τοῖς διδύμοις σου τέκνοις ἐπὶ χρόνον τινά, μέχρις ὅτε μηνύσω ἐπανελθεῖν σε ἐνταῦθα, ἔκβηθι τὴν πόλιν, ἐπεὶ ἅμα ἀνδρὶ καὶ πᾶσίν σου τοῖς τέκνοις αἰφνιδίως κακῶς τελευτήσεις. ὁμῶς οὕτως ἐποίησα. ἅμα γὰρ τῷ τὸν ὄνειρον ψεύσασθαί με τῷ ἀνδρὶ αὐτὸς περίφοβος γενόμενος μετὰ τῶν ἐμῶν δύο υἱῶν δούλων τε καὶ παιδισκῶν καὶ χρημάτων συχνῶν κατὰ πλοῦν εἰς Ἀθήνας με ἐξέπεμψεν ἐκπαιδεῦσαι τοὺς υἱούς, μέχρις ἂν (ἔφη) τῷ χρηματίσαντι δόξῃ ἐπανιέναι σε πρὸς ἐμέ. ὁμῶς ἅμα τέκνοις ἡ τάλαινα πλέουσα ὑπὸ ἀνέμων ἀταξίας εἰς τούτους ἀπορριφεῖσα τοὺς τόπους, νυκτὸς τῆς νηὸς διαλυθείσης, ναυφραγίῳ περιέπεσα. πάντων δὲ θανόντων ἡ ἀτυχὴς ἐγὼ μόνη ὑπὸ σφοδροῦ κύματος ῥιπισθεῖσα ἐπὶ πέτρας ἐρρίφην, ἐφ’ ἧς καθεσθεῖσα ἡ ἀθλία ἐλπίδι τοῦ τὰ τέκνα με ζῶντα εὑρεῖν εἰς τὸν βυθὸν ἐμαυτὴν οὐκ ἔρριψα τότε ὅτε τὴν ψυχὴν μεμεθυσμένην τοῖς κύμασιν ἔχουσα τοῦτο ποιῆσαι ῥᾳδίως ἐδυνάμην.

πλὴν ἐπειδὴ ὄρθρος ἐγένετο, μεγάλα βοῶσα καὶ γοερὰ κωκύουσα περιεβλεπόμην, ζητοῦσα τῶν ἐμῶν ταλαιπώρων βρεφῶν τὰ νεκρὰ σώματα. ἐλεήσαντες οὖν με οἱ ἐπιχώριοι, γυμνὴν ἰδόντες ἐνδύσαντές με τὸ πρῶτον, τὸν βυθὸν ἀνηραύνων, τὰ ἐμὰ ζητοῦντες τέκνα. καὶ ἐπεὶ μηδὲν ηὕρισκον ὧν ἐζήτουν, παραμυθίας χάριν τινὲς τῶν φιλοξένων γυναικῶν προσελθοῦσαι διηγοῦντο ἑκάστη τὰ ἑαυτῆς κακά, ἵνα τῇ τῶν ὁμοίων συμφορᾷ παραμυθίας τύχω, ὃ δὴ μᾶλλόν με ἐλύπει. οὐ γὰρ ἔφην οὕτω κακὴ εἶναι ὡς ταῖς ἄλλων συμφοραῖς παραμυθίας τύχω. καὶ δὴ εἰς ξενίαν πολλῶν με ἄγειν ἀξιουσῶν μία τις τῶν ἐνταῦθα πενιχρὰ πολὺ βιασαμένη εἰς τὸ ἑαυτῆς ἐλθεῖν ἠνάγκασε σκήνωμα, εἰποῦσά μοι Θάρρει, γύναι· καὶ γὰρ ὁ ἐμὸς ἀνὴρ ναύτης ὢν κατὰ θάλασσαν τέθνηκεν, ἐν τῇ νεαζούσῃ τυγχάνων ἡλικίᾳ· καὶ ἔκτοτε πολλῶν με ἀξιούντων πρὸς γάμον ἐγὼ χηρεύειν εἱλόμην, τὸν ἐμὸν ποθοῦσα ἄνδρα. ἔσται δὲ ἡμῖν κοινὰ ἃ διὰ χειρῶν ἀμφότεραι πορίζειν δυνάμεθα.

καὶ ἵνα μή σοι μηκύνω τοὺς οὐκ ἀναγκαίους λόγους, συνῴκησα αὐτῇ διὰ τὴν φιλανδρίαν. καὶ μετ’ οὐ πολὺ ἐμοῦ τῆς ταλαιπώρου αἱ χεῖρες ὑπὸ τῶν δηγμάτων παρείθησαν, καὶ ἡ ὑποδεξαμένη με γυνὴ ὅλη ὑπὸ πάθους τινὸς συνδεθεῖσα ἐπὶ τῆς οἰκίας ἔρριπται. ἐπεὶ οὖν ὁ τῶν πάλαι γυναικῶν ἔλεος παρήκμασεν, ἐγὼ δὲ καὶ ἡ κατ’ οἶκον ἀμφότεραι ἐπισινεῖς τυγχάνομεν: ἐκ πολλῶν χρόνων ἐνταῦθα (ὡς ὁρᾷς) καθέζομαι προσαιτοῦσα καὶ ὧν ἂν εὐπορήσω, καὶ τῇ συνταλαιπώρῳ εἰς τροφὰς κομίζω. καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐμὰ ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον αὐτάρκως εἰρήσθω· λοιπὸν σὺ κωλύεις τὴν ὑπόσχεσιν πληρῶσαι τοῦ δοῦναι τὸ φάρμακον, ὅπως κἀκείνῃ ἐπιθυμούσῃ θανεῖν δῶ καὶ οὕτως κἀγὼ τοῦ ζῆν (ὡς ἔφης) μεταλλάξαι δυνηθῶ.

ταῦτα τῆς γυναικὸς εἰπούσης ὑπὸ λογισμῶν πολλῶν ὁ Πέτρος μετέωρος ἐδόκει ἵστασθαι. ἐγὼ δὲ ἐπελθὼν ἔφην Ἐκ πολλοῦ σε περιερχόμενος ζητῶ, καὶ τὰ νῦν τί ποιοῦμεν; ὁ δὲ Πέτρος προσέταξέν μοι προάξαντι μένειν αὐτὸν ἐπὶ τοῦ σκάφους. καὶ ἐπειδὴ ἀντειπεῖν οὐκ ἦν αὐτῷ κελεύσαντι, ἐποίησα τὸ προσταχθέν. ὁ δὲ Πέτρος μικρᾷ τινὶ ὑποψίᾳ (ὡς αὐτός μοι πάντα ὕστερον διηγήσατο) παλλόμενος τὴν καρδίαν ἐπυνθάνετο τῆς γυναικὸς λέγων Εἰπέ μοι, γύναι, τὸ γένος καὶ τὴν πόλιν καὶ τῶν τέκνων τὰ ὀνόματα, καὶ ἤδη δίδωμί σοι τὸ φάρμακον. ἡ δὲ βίαν πάσχουσα καὶ εἰπεῖν οὐ θέλουσα, τὸ δὲ φάρμακον λαβεῖν ἐπιθυμοῦσα, ἐσοφίσατο ἄλλα ἀντὶ ἄλλων εἰπεῖν καὶ ὁμῶς ἔφη αὐτὴν μὲν ἐφεσίαν εἶναι, τὸν δὲ ἄνδρα Σικελόν, ὁμῶς καὶ τῶν τριῶν τέκνων ἤλλαξεν τὰ ὀνόματα. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος νομίσας αὐτὴν ἀληθεύειν ἔφη Οἴμοι, γύναι· ἐνόμιζον μεγάλην τινὰ χαρὰν τὴν σήμερον ἄγειν ἡμέραν, ὑποπτεύσας σὲ τινὰ εἶναι, ἣν ἐνόμιζον, ἧς τὰ πράγματα ἀκούσας ἀκριβῶς ἐπίσταμαι. ἡ δὲ ἐξώρκιζεν λέγουσα Δέομαι εἰπέ μοι, ἵνα εἰδῶ εἴ ἔστιν τις ἐν γυναιξὶν ἀθλιωτέρα ἐμοῦ.

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ψεύδεσθαι οὐκ εἰδὼς ὑπὸ ἐλέους τοῦ πρὸς αὐτὴν τὸ ἀληθὲς λέγειν ἤρξατο Ἐμοί τις λοιπὸν ἤδη νεανίας ὢν παρέπεται, τῶν τῆς θεοσεβείας ὀρεγόμενος λόγων, Ῥωμαίων ὑπάρχων πολίτης, ὅστις μοι διηγεῖται πῶς πατέρα ἔχων καὶ ἀδελφοὺς δύο διδύμους οὐδένα τούτων ὁρᾷ· ἥ τε γὰρ μήτηρ (φησίν), ὡς ὁ πατὴρ διηγεῖτό μοι, ὄνειρον ἰδοῦσα τὴν Ῥωμαίων πόλιν ἐπὶ χρόνον τινὰ ἐξῆλθεν μετὰ τῶν διδύμων αὐτῆς τέκνων, ἵνα μὴ κακῷ μόρῳ τελευτήσῃ, καὶ σὺν αὐτοῖς ἐκβᾶσα οὐχ εὑρίσκεται. ὁ δὲ ταύτης μὲν ἀνήρ, αὐτοῦ δὲ πατὴρ καὶ αὐτὸς εἰς ἐπιζήτησιν αὐτῆς ἐκβὰς οὐχ εὑρίσκεται.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: However, so that these things might happen in this way, I devised the fabrication of a dream, as though someone had stood beside me at night and said, “Woman, leave the city immediately with your twin children for a time, until I tell you to return here, for you will suddenly die a terrible death together with your husband and all your children.” All the same, I did so. For as soon as I falsely told my husband about the dream, he himself became terrified and sent me by sea to Athens, together with my two sons, male and female servants, and a considerable amount of money, so that I might educate my sons, “until,” he said, “the one who gave the revelation decides that you should return to me.” Yet while I, wretched as I am, was sailing with my children, I was driven into these parts by unruly winds; when the ship broke apart in the night, I suffered shipwreck. After everyone else had died, I alone, unfortunate woman that I am, was swept along by a fierce wave and thrown onto a rock. Seated on it, wretched as I was, I did not cast myself into the deep, because I hoped to find my children alive—not even then, when my soul was intoxicated by the waves and I could easily have done it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I devised the fabrication of a dream
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase means that she deliberately conceived a plan to fabricate a dream, not that she merely interpreted or experienced one.

lexical_decisions.chosen: All the same, I did so
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contextual rendering treats ὁμῶς concessively, like ὅμως, although the printed form can lexically suggest “likewise” or “in the same way.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: male and female servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: The reader-facing wording follows the supplied policy, but the Greek terms denote enslaved male and female household members—male slaves and female slaves or slave maids—not merely free hired workers.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who gave the revelation
lexical_decisions.rationale: χρηματίζω here concerns the supernatural communication in the alleged dream; alternatives include “the one who gave the warning” or “the one who delivered the oracle.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: by unruly winds
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, the wording evokes being driven by the disorder or unruliness of winds.

lexical_decisions.chosen: thrown onto a rock. Seated on it
lexical_decisions.rationale: πέτρας is understood as genitive singular after ἐπί, agreeing with singular ἧς; taking it as accusative plural would produce a number mismatch.

lexical_decisions.chosen: my soul was intoxicated by the waves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the metaphor of the soul made drunk or overwhelmed by the waves.

passages.text: However, when daybreak came, I kept looking around, crying loudly and wailing mournfully, searching for the dead bodies of my unfortunate babies. The local people took pity on me. Seeing that I was naked, they first clothed me and then searched the deep for my children. When they found none of what they were seeking, some of the hospitable women approached me for the sake of comfort, and each recounted her own troubles, so that through the shared experience of similar misfortune I might find comfort—which in fact grieved me even more. For I said that I was not so wicked as to find comfort in the misfortunes of others. Although many offered to take me in as a guest, one poor woman from this place pressed me so insistently that she compelled me to come to her own shelter. She said to me, “Take courage, woman. My husband too was a sailor and died at sea while still in the bloom of youth. Since then, although many have sought me in marriage, I have chosen to remain a widow because I long for my husband. Whatever both of us can procure by the work of our hands will be shared between us.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: my unfortunate babies
lexical_decisions.rationale: βρέφη denotes infants or very young children; “babies” retains that force rather than harmonizing it with the earlier designation “sons.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: searched the deep
lexical_decisions.rationale: The local people search the sea’s depth for the missing children; “searched the bottom” is another possible rendering. The printed singular participle is disclosed separately as an agreement irregularity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ ἔφην οὕτω κακὴ εἶναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: I was not so wicked
lexical_decisions.rationale: In context she rejects obtaining comfort from others’ suffering, so κακή has a moral sense. “So miserable” is lexically possible but less coherent with the following clause.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς ξενίαν πολλῶν με ἄγειν ἀξιουσῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: although many offered to take me in as a guest
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξενία refers to hospitality or lodging for a stranger; the wording may also be rendered “many asked to bring me into their homes.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: while still in the bloom of youth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase describes the husband as being at a youthful age when he died.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἃ διὰ χειρῶν ἀμφότεραι πορίζειν δυνάμεθα
lexical_decisions.chosen: whatever both of us can procure by the work of our hands
lexical_decisions.rationale: διὰ χειρῶν points to what they can obtain through their own manual labor.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐλεήσαντες οὖν με οἱ ἐπιχώριοι, γυμνὴν ἰδόντες ἐνδύσαντές με τὸ πρῶτον, τὸν βυθὸν ἀνηραύνων, τὰ ἐμὰ ζητοῦντες τέκνα.
source_issues.issue: The image-checked selected edition prints the nominative singular participle ἀνηραύνων amid plural participles governed by the plural subject οἱ ἐπιχώριοι. This is an apparent agreement irregularity, but the surrounding plural forms make the local people the defensible agent of the search.

passages.text: And, so that I do not prolong for you words that are unnecessary, I lived with her because of her devotion to her husband. Before long, my hands—wretched woman that I am—were paralyzed by attacks of biting pain, and the woman who had taken me in, her whole body bound by some affliction, lies prostrate at home. Since, then, the compassion of the women from before has waned, and both I and the woman at home are incapacitated, for many years I have sat here, as you see, begging; and whatever I manage to obtain, I also carry home as food for my fellow sufferer. So much for my own affairs; let them have been told sufficiently. What remains is that you are preventing the fulfillment of your promise to give me the drug, so that I may give it to her as well, since she desires to die, and in this way I too may be able to depart from life, as you said.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of her devotion to her husband
lexical_decisions.rationale: φιλανδρία denotes love of or devotion to a husband. The immediate context favors the poor widow’s devotion, though the phrase could encompass the narrator’s corresponding marital devotion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: were paralyzed by attacks of biting pain
lexical_decisions.rationale: δήγματα literally denotes bites or stings and can describe sharp, biting pains; a more literal alternative is “were disabled by the bites.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: her whole body bound by some affliction
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὅλη indicates that the affliction affected her wholly, while συνδεθεῖσα retains the image of being bound.

lexical_decisions.chosen: lies prostrate at home
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect ἔρριπται presents the resulting prostrate condition as continuing at the time of the woman’s account; “has been laid prostrate at home” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐγὼ δὲ καὶ ἡ κατ’ οἶκον ἀμφότεραι ἐπισινεῖς τυγχάνομεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: both I and the woman at home are incapacitated
lexical_decisions.rationale: The present τυγχάνομεν describes both women as currently harmed, impaired, or afflicted, explaining their continuing need.

lexical_decisions.chosen: whatever I manage to obtain
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐπορέω here concerns securing available resources rather than being generally wealthy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the drug
lexical_decisions.rationale: φάρμακον can mean medicine, drug, or poison. “Drug” preserves the lexical breadth, while the expressed desire for death supplies the lethal purpose in context.

lexical_decisions.chosen: depart from life
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction is a euphemism for dying, literally involving a change or departure from living.

passages.text: When the woman had said this, Peter seemed, amid many thoughts, to stand suspended. I came up and said, “I have been going around looking for you for a long time. What are we to do now?” Peter instructed me to go on ahead and wait for him at the boat. Since there was no contradicting him when he gave an order, I did what had been commanded. But Peter, his heart throbbing with a faint suspicion—as he himself related everything to me later—questioned the woman, saying, “Tell me, woman, your origin and city and the names of your children, and I will give you the drug at once.” She was caught under pressure, unwilling to tell him but eager to receive the drug, so she contrived to say one thing in place of another. Even so, she said that she herself was an Ephesian and that her husband was a Sicilian; she likewise changed the names of all three children. Peter, thinking that she was telling the truth, said, “Alas, woman! I thought that today would be a day of great joy, because I suspected that you were a certain woman—the one I thought you were—whose circumstances I have heard and know exactly.” She adjured him, saying, “I beg you, tell me, so that I may know whether there is any woman more miserable than I am.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ λογισμῶν πολλῶν ὁ Πέτρος μετέωρος ἐδόκει ἵστασθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: Peter seemed, amid many thoughts, to stand suspended
lexical_decisions.rationale: μετέωρος preserves an image of being suspended or unsettled; idiomatic alternatives include “stood perplexed” or “was lost in thought.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: your origin and city
lexical_decisions.rationale: γένος may refer to family, people, nationality, or origin. “Origin” leaves the scope open alongside the more specific request for her city.

lexical_decisions.chosen: caught under pressure
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase depicts her as constrained by conflicting pressures: reluctance to disclose the truth and desire to obtain the drug. More literally, it can mean “suffering compulsion.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: she contrived to say one thing in place of another
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom describes an ingenious evasion or lie while retaining the source’s wording pattern.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Even so, she said
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contextual rendering treats ὁμῶς concessively, like ὅμως. “Likewise” is possible for the printed form but fits the progression less well.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁμῶς καὶ τῶν τριῶν τέκνων ἤλλαξεν τὰ ὀνόματα
lexical_decisions.chosen: she likewise changed the names of all three children
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here the same printed adverb naturally coordinates the alteration of the children’s names with the false statements about her own and her husband’s origins.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑποπτεύσας σὲ τινὰ εἶναι, ἣν ἐνόμιζον
lexical_decisions.chosen: because I suspected that you were a certain woman—the one I thought you were
lexical_decisions.rationale: The deliberately repetitive rendering preserves Peter’s guarded identification. A smoother alternative is “suspecting you were someone I had in mind.”

passages.text: And Peter, who did not know how to lie, began out of compassion for her to tell the truth: “A certain person, by now a young man, accompanies me—a Roman citizen who desires teachings about reverence for God. He tells me how, though he has a father and two twin brothers, he sees none of them. ‘For my mother,’ he says, ‘as my father used to tell me, saw a dream and left the city of the Romans for a time with her twin children, so that she would not die by an evil fate; and after leaving with them, she has not been found.’ The husband of this woman—who is the young man’s father—himself also left to search for her and has not been found.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: who did not know how to lie
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase describes Peter as unpracticed or incapable in lying, not merely as unaware that a particular statement was false.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by now a young man
lexical_decisions.rationale: λοιπὸν ἤδη marks his present stage of life. Alternatives include “now already a young man” and “now at last a young man.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: who desires teachings about reverence for God
lexical_decisions.rationale: θεοσέβεια is piety or reverence directed toward God, while λόγοι here denotes words, discourses, or teachings.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἥ τε γὰρ μήτηρ (φησίν), ὡς ὁ πατὴρ διηγεῖτό μοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: ‘For my mother,’ he says, ‘as my father used to tell me’
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering treats μοι as retained first-person wording within the young man’s embedded report. A formally indirect alternative, “his mother ... as the father told me,” would make “me” refer to Peter, which is contextually difficult.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the city of the Romans
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the source’s descriptive expression rather than replacing it silently with the conventional name “Rome.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: die by an evil fate
lexical_decisions.rationale: μόρος denotes fate, doom, or the death allotted by fate; “meet a terrible death” is a smoother alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ δὲ ταύτης μὲν ἀνήρ, αὐτοῦ δὲ πατὴρ
lexical_decisions.chosen: The husband of this woman—who is the young man’s father
lexical_decisions.rationale: The paired description identifies the same person in relation first to the woman and then to the accompanying young man.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ αὐτὸς εἰς ἐπιζήτησιν αὐτῆς ἐκβὰς
lexical_decisions.chosen: himself also left to search for her
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording preserves both the emphatic αὐτός and the purpose expressed by εἰς ἐπιζήτησιν αὐτῆς.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
